messages.content: You are a Spanish writing tutor. You help writers make their posts say what they mean, for the people who will read them.

Target language: Spanish. The writer's own language: English.
Where it will be posted: Email to a Spanish language school. Who will read it: The school's admissions contact, Sra. Morales. What the writer wants to do: Applying for the September course and asking about prices and housing.
The writer's draft. A separate pass fixes its small language errors (grammar, articles, tense, wrong words); ignore those. Passages in English are things the writer could not yet say; "a/b" marks a choice they have not made. Sentences are numbered:
[S1] Estimada Sra.
[S2] Morales:

[S3] Mi nombre es Daniel y yo soy de Manchester, en Inglaterra.
[S4] Le escribo porque quiero aplicar para el curso de septiembre.
[S5] Vengo por mejorar mi español: mi novia es de Granada, conocí a su familia el año pasado pero no entendí casi nada, y estoy muy excitado de aprender para poder hablar con ellos.

[S6] ¿Es posible que usted me envía información sobre los precios?
[S7] También tengo algunas preguntas.
[S8] Primero, prefiero una habitación con familia / un piso compartido, no sé cual es mejor para aprender.
[S9] ¿Es el piso cerca de la escuela?
[S10] Necesito una habitación tranquilo para estudiar.
[S11] Segundo, ¿puedo traer mi bicicleta?
[S12] Me gusta montar en bici y quiero explorar las montañas.
[S13] Tercero, soy vegetariano (I'm not picky but I don't eat meat) y espero que la familia puede cocinar algo para mí.
[S14] Mi novia viene conmigo el primer fin de semana.

[S15] ¿Me puedes decir cuándo empiezan los cursos?
[S16] Necesito una respuesta antes de fin de mes porque tengo que comprar el vuelo.
[S17] Estoy seguro de que voy a tener un buen tiempo en su escuela.
[S18] Mirando adelante a oír de usted.

[S19] Saludos,
[S20] Daniel Clarke
The first pass left these words as the writer wrote them, because fixing them needs something only the writer can decide; each must be inside one of your spots: «prefiero una habitación con familia / un piso compartido»; «(I'm not picky but I don't eat meat)»; «Necesito una respuesta antes de fin de mes porque tengo que comprar el vuelo.»; «Mirando adelante a oír de usted.».

A fluent writer's version of the same post, for comparison (not to be copied wholesale):
<<<
Estimada Sra. Morales:

Me llamo Daniel Clarke y vivo en Manchester, Inglaterra. Me gustaría apuntarme al curso que empieza en septiembre. Quiero mejorar mi español porque mi novia es de Granada. El año pasado conocí a su familia y apenas entendí nada de lo que decían, así que tengo muchísimas ganas de poder charlar con ellos de verdad.

¿Podría enviarme información sobre los precios, por favor? También tengo algunas dudas sobre el alojamiento. Estoy entre quedarme con una familia o en un piso compartido, pero no sé cuál me ayudaría más a aprender. ¿El piso queda cerca de la escuela? Necesito un sitio tranquilo para estudiar.

Además, quería preguntarle si puedo llevar mi bici. Me encanta salir en bici y me apetece mucho recorrer las montañas. Otra cosa: soy vegetariano (no soy nada exigente, pero no como carne). ¿Sería posible que la familia me preparara algo sin carne? Mi novia vendrá a verme el primer fin de semana.

¿Me podría decir cuándo empiezan los cursos? Necesito saberlo antes de final de mes, porque tengo que comprar el billete de avión. Estoy seguro de que lo voy a pasar muy bien en su escuela.

Muchas gracias por su tiempo. Espero su respuesta.

Atentamente,
Daniel Clarke
>>>

Small language errors are handled separately. Now find every place worth a second pass. There are two kinds of spot.

kind "meaning": the post cannot do its job until the writer decides something only they know:
- passages still in English that are whole clauses (the writer will build them in Spanish themselves), and "a/b" choices;
- a point the reader needs but the post leaves unstated (a conclusion the evidence is meant to support, the actual question);
- a connective or framing word whose relation (contrast, concession, cause, addition) does not match the ideas it joins, or whose other half never comes;
- wording that readers could take another way than the writer means, as defined below;
- wording off in register, as defined below: read as meant, but not how to speak to these readers.

kind "formulation": the meaning comes through, but a fluent writer would package it differently, and the difference is worth learning: the order of information, where the emphasis falls, a comparison that is not like for like, chains of nouns where Spanish would use a verb or a clause, an image, joke or set phrase carried over from English that a Spanish reader would take literally or not recognise, praise or criticism framed from an angle this community would not use, quoted or reported words not built into the sentence, a sentence or passage carrying too much at once. Compare each sentence with the fluent version above: where that version is built differently (not just a word swapped), decide whether the difference teaches something. List every such place; the writer will skip what they do not want. Word-level fixes with one obvious answer are not spots.

Words are taken another way than meant when a reader, reaching them, would come away with a different
- attitude or feeling: praise heard as a complaint, impatience or sarcasm; warmth as coldness; a joke as an insult; criticism heard as much harsher or milder than meant;
- act: a wish or hope heard as a demand, a question as a claim, news as a request, or the reverse;
- claim: who did what, what happened, what the writer thinks or knows (for example, that they misunderstood the work);
- strength: far stronger or weaker than meant (mild surprise heard as shock, a small doubt as rejection, liking as indifference).
It counts even when the rest of the post lets a careful reader work the intent out afterwards: words are read before what follows them, and a reader who first feels criticised, pushed or misjudged has been misread, however briefly (a friend told "you've really changed" hears a reproach before the next sentence makes it a compliment). It does not count when the difference would not change how the reader feels about the post or how they would answer: a shade of tone, a synonym, words that readers of this community take exactly as meant.

Words are off in register when they are read as meant but do not suit who is speaking to whom here, by the writer's relationship to the readers and this community's manners: too demanding or pushy (a reader telling an author what to do or how fast to write; a student giving a professor a deadline), too blunt or curt, too familiar, or too stiff and formal for the place, or presuming what is not theirs to decide (unasked criticism, telling an author what their characters should do). It counts even when some people here write that way: what matters is how the one addressed feels on receiving it (pressured, talked down to, put off, kept at a distance). Casual style that this place expects is not off in register.

Skip anything that is a matter of taste only. One spot per problem: two problems in neighbouring sentences are two spots.

A figure the writer made on purpose (a parallel or echo that turns the same word on something new, a deliberate repetition, wordplay) is judged by its words. If they are what a fluent writer would use, it is the writer's voice and never a spot by itself. If a word in it is not (a Spanish reader would stop at it), that word is a spot like any other, and its problem says both that the figure works and why that word does not.

For each spot, in this order:
- kind.
- quote: the exact words of the draft where a reader first stumbles, copied character for character: a few words inside one sentence.
- problem: in English, as the tutor who just read it, one or two sentences: starting from the quoted words, what a Spanish reader expects or understands on reaching them and why (what those words normally do in Spanish), and what is then missing, off or hard to follow. Specific to these words; never the fix or the better wording, which the writer will find themselves.
- scope: what the writer will rewrite, the smallest unit the problem and their decision affect: "words" (only the quoted words), "sentence" (the sentence containing them) or "sentences" (several neighbouring sentences, for a passage that carries too much or is ordered badly; list them in sentences).
- sentences: the numbers of the sentences the scope covers.
- question: the one thing the writer must tell you about what they mean here, as a short English question.
- mode and readings: what the writer might mean, in English. Readings must be genuinely different meanings that would be written differently in Spanish; if there is no second reading like that, give one. mode "one" when one reading is clearly the likeliest (put it first); mode "ask" when the writer must choose. A reading's label is that reading in a few words (about six Chinese characters or three words), what the writer taps to say "this one"; never a letter or a number.

Also give the post's argument map: the steps of what the post does, in order, each pointing at its sentences, status "missing" (with sentences []) for a step the reader needs but the post leaves out, "fix" for a step that is there but does not work yet. role is a label that fits in about six Chinese characters or twelve Latin letters (one to three short words); what says the step in at most about twelve words; note, only for fix and missing, says in one short sentence what is wrong.

All writer-facing text (gist, role, what, note, problem, question, readings) in English, short.

Work in two steps.

Step 1. Under "### ARGUMENT", write out in plain prose what this writer is trying to get across, step by step, including the steps and the real question they leave implicit. Then say, for each step, whether a reader who has only the post would get it.

Step 2. Under "### JSON", give the analysis:
First fill scan: one row for every numbered sentence, in order, with the matching words from the fluent version and whether it is built the same (none), differs only in words (word), or is built differently (structure). Every structure row must then be judged for a formulation spot.
{"scan":[{"s":1,"fluent":"the words in the fluent version that say what sentence 1 says","differs":"none|word|structure"}],"gist":"what the post is really asking or saying","map":[{"role":"...","what":"...","sentences":[1],"status":"ok|fix|missing","note":"..."}],"spots":[{"kind":"meaning|formulation","quote":"exact words","problem":"...","scope":"words|sentence|sentences","sentences":[1],"question":"...","mode":"one|ask","readings":[{"label":"...","meaning":"..."}]}]}

result.text:
### ARGUMENT

Daniel wants to apply for the September course at the school. He wants Sra. Morales to send prices and tell him when the courses start, because he must book his flight and needs an answer before the end of the month. He also has housing questions. He wants to learn Spanish so he can talk with his girlfriend's family in Granada. He has to choose between a host family and a shared flat, and he asks whether the flat is near the school and needs a quiet room to study. He asks whether he can bring his bicycle, since he wants to explore the mountains. He is vegetarian and hopes the family can cook meat-free meals. His girlfriend will visit the first weekend. He closes by hoping for a reply.

Step by step, for a reader who has only the post:
- Identity and origin (S3): clear.
- Purpose, applying for September (S4): clear, though "aplicar para" is an English-shaped verb.
- Reason for learning (S5): partly clear. The sentence packs several ideas together, and "excitado" may be read wrongly.
- Asking for prices (S6): clear, but phrased as a question about possibility, which is indirect.
- Housing choice (S8-S9): not clear. The writer has not chosen between the two options, so the follow-up question about the flat does not yet fit.
- Bicycle (S11-S12): clear.
- Diet (S13): not clear in Spanish. The English parenthetical is unresolved, and the hope is framed as an expectation of the family.
- Girlfriend's visit (S14): unclear. The reader cannot tell whether she is only visiting or will stay in the housing.
- Start date and deadline (S15-S16): partly clear. The deadline is stated, but the wording sounds demanding and the register is too familiar.
- Closing (S17-S18): the content is there, but both phrases are carried over from English.

The real question is whether Sra. Morales can send prices and the September start date soon, and whether the school can offer the housing Daniel needs.
